children.proof_nl:
Let J_t := (f_s : a+1 <= s <= t) for t = a, a+1, ..., b, with J_a := (0), and let B_t := R/J_t. Then B_a = R and B_b = A. Since every f_s is homogeneous, each J_t is a homogeneous ideal, so each B_t is a graded Q-algebra. Also each degree piece (B_t)_n is finite-dimensional over Q because it is a quotient of R_n.

First compute the Hilbert series of R. The monomials product_{s=a+1}^b x_s^{e_s}, with e_s in Z_{>=0}, form a Q-basis of R, and such a monomial has degree sum_{s=a+1}^b s e_s. Hence R_n has basis indexed by tuples (e_s) with sum s e_s = n; there are only finitely many such tuples because all s are positive. Therefore
Hilb_R(q) = sum_{(e_s)} q^(sum s e_s)
= product_{s=a+1}^b (sum_{m >= 0} q^(m s))
= product_{s=a+1}^b 1/(1 - q^s).

Now fix t with a+1 <= t <= b, and put d_t := r + t. Since t >= a+1 >= 1 and r >= 0, we have d_t > 0. Because the ordered list (f_{a+1}, f_{a+2}, ..., f_b) is a regular sequence, the class of f_t in B_{t-1} is a non-zero-divisor. Moreover B_t = B_{t-1}/(f_t), where (f_t) now denotes the ideal of B_{t-1} generated by the class of f_t. Since f_t is homogeneous of degree d_t, for each n >= 0 the degree-n part of that ideal is exactly f_t (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t}, with the convention (B_{t-1})_m = 0 for m < 0. Thus for each n >= 0 we have an exact sequence of Q-vector spaces
0 -> (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t} -- multiplication by f_t -> (B_{t-1})_n -> (B_t)_n -> 0.
Therefore
dim_Q (B_t)_n = dim_Q (B_{t-1})_n - dim_Q (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t}.
Summing over n >= 0 gives
Hilb_{B_t}(q) = (1 - q^(d_t)) Hilb_{B_{t-1}}(q).

Iterating this identity from t = a+1 up to t = b, and using the formula for Hilb_R(q), we obtain
Hilb_A(q) = Hilb_{B_b}(q)
= (product_{s=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+s))) Hilb_R(q)
= product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)).

By the definition of Hilbert series, this means that for every j >= 0, the coefficient of q^j in product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)) is exactly dim_Q A_j. In particular, every such coefficient is a nonnegative integer.

It remains to prove that A is finite-dimensional. For any real u with 0 < u < 1, the series sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) u^n converges because dim_Q A_n <= dim_Q R_n and
sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q R_n) u^n = product_{s=a+1}^b 1/(1 - u^s) < infinity.
So we may evaluate the identity above at such a real u:
sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) u^n = product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - u^(r+s))/(1 - u^s)).

For each fixed s,
(1 - u^m)/(1 - u) = 1 + u + ... + u^(m-1),
so
lim_{u -> 1^-} (1 - u^(r+s))/(1 - u^s) = (r+s)/s.
Hence the right-hand side has a finite limit product_{s=a+1}^b ((r+s)/s) as u -> 1^-; in particular it stays bounded near u = 1.

Suppose, for contradiction, that A_n != 0 for infinitely many n. Then there are infinitely many n with a_n := dim_Q A_n >= 1. Given any positive integer N, choose distinct indices n_1 < ... < n_N with a_{n_i} >= 1. For u sufficiently close to 1, we have u^{n_i} > 1/2 for all i, and then
sum_{n >= 0} a_n u^n >= sum_{i=1}^N u^{n_i} > N/2.
Since N is arbitrary, the left-hand side would be unbounded as u -> 1^-, contradicting the boundedness of the right-hand side. Therefore A_n = 0 for all but finitely many n. As each A_n is finite-dimensional, A = direct sum_{n >= 0} A_n is finite-dimensional over Q.

Thus A is a finite-dimensional graded Q-algebra, its Hilbert series is exactly product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)), and the coefficient of q^j in that product is dim_Q A_j and hence a nonnegative integer for every j >= 0.

Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Put A := R / (f_s : s in I), and let A_n denote the degree-n homogeneous component of A. Then A is a finite-dimensional graded Q-algebra and its Hilbert series is
Hilb_A(q) = sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) q^n = product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)).
In particular, for every integer j >= 0, the coefficient [q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) equals dim_Q A_j and is a nonnegative integer.

children.proof_nl:
Let
F(q) := product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = product_{s in I} ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)).
We interpret [q^j] in the formal power series ring Z[[q]]. This is legitimate because every s in I satisfies s >= a+1 >= 1.

For each s in I,
(1 - q^s)^(-1) = sum_{m>=0} q^(ms)
in Z[[q]], since multiplying the right-hand side by 1 - q^s gives 1. Hence
product_{s in I} (1 - q^s)^(-1) = product_{s in I} sum_{m_s>=0} q^(m_s s).
Because I is finite, expanding this finite product gives
product_{s in I} (1 - q^s)^(-1) = sum_{(m_s)_{s in I}} q^(sum_{s in I} m_s s),
where the sum runs over all tuples of nonnegative integers (m_s) indexed by I.

Likewise,
product_{s in I} (1 - q^(r+s))
= sum_{S subseteq I} product_{s in S} (-q^(r+s))
= sum_{S subseteq I} (-1)^{|S|} q^(sum_{s in S} (r+s)).

Multiplying the two expansions, we obtain in Z[[q]]
F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} sum_{(m_s)_{s in I}} (-1)^{|S|} q^( sum_{s in S}(r+s) + sum_{s in I} m_s s ).

Now fix j >= 0. Only finitely many terms on the right can contribute to the coefficient of q^j: the set I is finite, and if sum_{s in I} m_s s <= j then for each s in I we have 0 <= m_s <= j/s. Therefore we may read off the coefficient term-by-term:
[q^j] F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} (-1)^{|S|} * #{ (m_s)_{s in I} : sum_{s in I} m_s s + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }.

For each fixed S, such tuples (m_s) are in bijection with finite multisets lambda of elements of I: m_s is the multiplicity of s in lambda. Under this bijection,
wt(lambda) = sum_{s in I} m_s s.
Therefore
#{ (m_s)_{s in I} : sum_{s in I} m_s s + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }
= #{ lambda : wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }.
Substituting this into the previous formula gives
[q^j] F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} sum_{lambda : wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j} (-1)^{|S|}.
But by definition, the pairs (S, lambda) appearing in this double sum are exactly the elements of X_j. Hence
[q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|},
as required.

Since 0 <= a <= b, the set I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b} has exactly b-a elements, so I is finite. Hence there are only finitely many subsets S of I, in fact exactly 2^(b-a) of them.

Fix one such subset S. Suppose (S, lambda) is in X_j. For each t in I, let m_t be the multiplicity of t in the finite multiset lambda. Because I is finite, the multiset lambda is uniquely determined by the tuple (m_t) indexed by t in I. Also,
wt(lambda) = sum_{t in I} t m_t = j - sum_{s in S}(r+s).
Now r >= 0, and every s in I satisfies s >= a+1 >= 1, so each term r+s is nonnegative. Therefore sum_{s in S}(r+s) >= 0, and hence wt(lambda) <= j.

For each t in I we have t >= 1, so
0 <= m_t <= t m_t <= sum_{u in I} u m_u = wt(lambda) <= j.
Thus each m_t is an integer in {0,1,...,j}. Since I has b-a elements, there are at most (j+1)^(b-a) possible tuples (m_t), and therefore at most (j+1)^(b-a) possible multisets lambda for this fixed S. Since there are only finitely many choices of S, we obtain
|X_j| <= 2^(b-a) (j+1)^(b-a) < infinity.
So X_j is finite.

Now define
X_j^even = {(S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even}
and
X_j^odd = {(S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd}.
These two sets are disjoint and their union is X_j. By the definitions of E_j and O_j, we have |X_j^even| = E_j and |X_j^odd| = O_j.

Because X_j is finite, we may split the finite sum over X_j according to this partition:
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|}
= sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^even} (-1)^{|S|} + sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^odd} (-1)^{|S|}.
If (S,lambda) lies in X_j^even, then (-1)^{|S|} = 1. If (S,lambda) lies in X_j^odd, then (-1)^{|S|} = -1. Hence
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|}
= sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^even} 1 + sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^odd} (-1)
= |X_j^even| - |X_j^odd|
= E_j - O_j.
This is exactly the claimed identity.

children.proof_nl:
Let
Z := {x in X : p(x) = 0}
and
O := {x in X : p(x) = 1}.
Because p maps X into {0,1}, every element of X lies in exactly one of Z or O. Thus X = Z ∪ O and Z ∩ O = ∅.

Since X is finite, the subsets Z and O are finite. Write
O = {o_1, ..., o_m},
Z = {z_1, ..., z_n},
for some integers m,n >= 0. The hypothesis says that the number of zero-labeled elements is at least the number of one-labeled elements, so n >= m.

Now define a map iota : X -> X as follows:
- for 1 <= i <= m, set iota(o_i) = z_i;
- for 1 <= i <= m, set iota(z_i) = o_i;
- for m < j <= n, set iota(z_j) = z_j.

This is well-defined because O and Z are disjoint, and every element of X is either some o_i or some z_j.

We check that iota is an involution.
- If x = o_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(z_i) = o_i = x.
- If x = z_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(o_i) = z_i = x.
- If x = z_j with m < j <= n, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(z_j) = z_j = x.
Hence iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X.

Next, suppose iota(x) != x. Then x is in one of the first two cases above.
- If x = o_i, then iota(x) = z_i, so
  p(iota(x)) = p(z_i) = 0 = 1 - 1 = 1 - p(o_i) = 1 - p(x).
- If x = z_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(x) = o_i, so
  p(iota(x)) = p(o_i) = 1 = 1 - 0 = 1 - p(z_i) = 1 - p(x).
Thus whenever iota(x) != x, we have p(iota(x)) = 1 - p(x).

Finally, if iota(x) = x, then x cannot be any o_i and cannot be any z_i with 1 <= i <= m; therefore x = z_j for some j with m < j <= n. Hence p(x) = 0.

So iota is an involution on X, every moved point is matched with a point of opposite label, and every fixed point has label 0. This is exactly the required conclusion.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any finite set X equipped with a binary labeling p, if there are at least as many zeros as ones, then X can be partitioned by an involution iota so that every moved point is matched with a point of the opposite label, and every fixed point has label 0.

if the number of x in X with p(x)=0 is at least the number of x in X with p(x)=1

such that for every x in X, iota applied twice to x equals x
and for every x in X, if iota(x) is not x then p(iota(x)) equals 1 minus p(x)

Then there exists a map iota : X -> X such that iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X, and such that: if iota(x) != x, then p(iota(x)) = 1 - p(x); and if iota(x) = x, then p(x) = 0.

Target: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2). Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Strategy summary: Realize the interval product as the Hilbert series of a graded complete intersection in a weighted polynomial ring. The divisibility-count hypothesis is used only in one bottleneck algebraic realization lemma. Once that realization is available, the coefficient of q^j becomes a graded dimension and is therefore nonnegative. A separate expansion lemma identifies the same coefficient with the signed count of X_j, and a finite-set pairing lemma converts the resulting excess of even-parity elements into the required involution on X_j.

Assembly skeleton: Use the divisibility inequalities only once, through the bottleneck realization lemma L1, to build a weighted complete intersection A whose Hilbert series is exactly the interval product in the theorem. By L2, the coefficient of q^j in that product is dim_Q A_j, hence is a nonnegative integer. Independently, L3 expands the same coefficient as the signed sum over X_j with sign (-1)^{|S|}. 2. lem_20260329120705_7e7a087b: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}, let R := Q[x_s : s in I] be graded by deg(x_s) = s, and let (f_s)_{s in I} be a family of homogeneous polynomials in R such that deg(f_s) = r+s for every s in I and the ordered list by increasing s is a regular sequence. Put A := R / (f_s : s in I), and let A_n denote the degree-n homogeneous component of A. Then A is a finite-dimensional graded Q-algebra and its Hilbert series is
Hilb_A(q) = sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) q^n = product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)).
In particular, for every integer j >= 0, the coefficient [q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) equals dim_Q A_j and is a nonnegative integer.
Let J_t := (f_s : a+1 <= s <= t) for t = a, a+1, ..., b, with J_a := (0), and let B_t := R/J_t. Then B_a = R and B_b = A. Since every f_s is homogeneous, each J_t is a homogeneous ideal, so each B_t is a graded Q-algebra. Also each degree piece (B_t)_n is finite-dimensional over Q because it is a quotient of R_n.\n\nFirst compute the Hilbert series of R. The monomials product_{s=a+1}^b x_s^{e_s}, with e_s in Z_{>=0}, form a Q-basis of R, and such a monomial has degree sum_{s=a+1}^b s e_s. Hence R_n has basis indexed by tuples (e_s) with sum s e_s = n; there are only finitely many such tuples because all s are positive. Therefore\nHilb_R(q) = sum_{(e_s)} q^(sum s e_s)\n= product_{s=a+1}^b (sum_{m >= 0} q^(m s))\n= product_{s=a+1}^b 1/(1 - q^s).\n\nNow fix t with a+1 <= t <= b, and put d_t := r + t. Since t >= a+1 >= 1 and r >= 0, we have d_t > 0. Because the ordered list (f_{a+1}, f_{a+2}, ..., f_b) is a regular sequence, the class of f_t in B_{t-1} is a non-zero-divisor. Moreover B_t = B_{t-1}/(f_t), where (f_t) now denotes the ideal of B_{t-1} generated by the class of f_t. Since f_t is homogeneous of degree d_t, for each n >= 0 the degree-n part of that ideal is exactly f_t (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t}, with the convention (B_{t-1})_m = 0 for m < 0. Thus for each n >= 0 we have an exact sequence of Q-vector spaces\n0 -> (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t} -- multiplication by f_t -> (B_{t-1})_n -> (B_t)_n -> 0.\nTherefore\ndim_Q (B_t)_n = dim_Q (B_{t-1})_n - dim_Q (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t}.\nSumming over n >= 0 gives\nHilb_{B_t}(q) = (1 - q^(d_t)) Hilb_{B_{t-1}}(q).\n\nIterating this identity from t = a+1 up to t = b, and using the formula for Hilb_R(q), we obtain\nHilb_A(q) = Hilb_{B_b}(q)\n= (product_{s=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+s))) Hilb_R(q)\n= product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)).\n\nBy the definition of Hilbert series, this means that for every j >= 0, the coefficient of q^j in product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)) is exactly dim_Q A_j. In particular, every such coefficient is a nonnegative integer.\n\nIt remains to prove that A is finite-dimensional. For any real u with 0 < u < 1, the series sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) u^n converges because dim_Q A_n <= dim_Q R_n and\nsum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q R_n) u^n = product_{s=a+1}^b 1/(1 - u^s) < infinity.\nSo we may evaluate the identity above at such a real u:\nsum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) u^n = product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - u^(r+s))/(1 - u^s)).\n\nFor each fixed s,\n(1 - u^m)/(1 - u) = 1 + u + ... + u^(m-1),\nso\nlim_{u -> 1^-} (1 - u^(r+s))/(1 - u^s) = (r+s)/s.\nHence the right-hand side has a finite limit product_{s=a+1}^b ((r+s)/s) as u -> 1^-; in particular it stays bounded near u = 1.\n\nSuppose, for contradiction, that A_n != 0 for infinitely many n. Then there are infinitely many n with a_n := dim_Q A_n >= 1. Given any positive integer N, choose distinct indices n_1 < ... < n_N with a_{n_i} >= 1. For u sufficiently close to 1, we have u^{n_i} > 1/2 for all i, and then\nsum_{n >= 0} a_n u^n >= sum_{i=1}^N u^{n_i} > N/2.\nSince N is arbitrary, the left-hand side would be unbounded as u -> 1^-, contradicting the boundedness of the right-hand side. Therefore A_n = 0 for all but finitely many n. As each A_n is finite-dimensional, A = direct sum_{n >= 0} A_n is finite-dimensional over Q.\n\nThus A is a finite-dimensional graded Q-algebra, its Hilbert series is exactly product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)), and the coefficient of q^j in that product is dim_Q A_j and hence a nonnegative integer for every j >= 0.

3. lem_20260329120722_adc74369: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define X_j to be the set of all pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, and wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j, where wt(lambda) denotes the sum of the elements of lambda. Then
[q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|},
where |S| is the cardinality of S.
Let
F(q) := product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = product_{s in I} ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)).
We interpret [q^j] in the formal power series ring Z[[q]]. This is legitimate because every s in I satisfies s >= a+1 >= 1.

For each s in I,
(1 - q^s)^(-1) = sum_{m>=0} q^(ms)
in Z[[q]], since multiplying the right-hand side by 1 - q^s gives 1. Hence
product_{s in I} (1 - q^s)^(-1) = product_{s in I} sum_{m_s>=0} q^(m_s s).
Because I is finite, expanding this finite product gives
product_{s in I} (1 - q^s)^(-1) = sum_{(m_s)_{s in I}} q^(sum_{s in I} m_s s),
where the sum runs over all tuples of nonnegative integers (m_s) indexed by I.

Likewise,
product_{s in I} (1 - q^(r+s))
= sum_{S subseteq I} product_{s in S} (-q^(r+s))
= sum_{S subseteq I} (-1)^{|S|} q^(sum_{s in S} (r+s)).

Multiplying the two expansions, we obtain in Z[[q]]
F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} sum_{(m_s)_{s in I}} (-1)^{|S|} q^( sum_{s in S}(r+s) + sum_{s in I} m_s s ).

Now fix j >= 0. Only finitely many terms on the right can contribute to the coefficient of q^j: the set I is finite, and if sum_{s in I} m_s s <= j then for each s in I we have 0 <= m_s <= j/s. Therefore we may read off the coefficient term-by-term:
[q^j] F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} (-1)^{|S|} * #{ (m_s)_{s in I} : sum_{s in I} m_s s + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }.

For each fixed S, such tuples (m_s) are in bijection with finite multisets lambda of elements of I: m_s is the multiplicity of s in lambda. Under this bijection,
wt(lambda) = sum_{s in I} m_s s.
Therefore
#{ (m_s)_{s in I} : sum_{s in I} m_s s + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }
= #{ lambda : wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }.
Substituting this into the previous formula gives
[q^j] F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} sum_{lambda : wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j} (-1)^{|S|}.
But by definition, the pairs (S, lambda) appearing in this double sum are exactly the elements of X_j. Hence
[q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|},
as required.

4. lem_20260329120747_f3501562: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define X_j to be the set of all pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, and wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j, where wt(lambda) is the sum of the elements of lambda. Then X_j is finite. If E_j is the number of elements (S,lambda) in X_j with |S| even and O_j is the number of elements (S,lambda) in X_j with |S| odd, then
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|} = E_j - O_j.
Since 0 <= a <= b, the set I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b} has exactly b-a elements, so I is finite. Hence there are only finitely many subsets S of I, in fact exactly 2^(b-a) of them.

Fix one such subset S. Suppose (S, lambda) is in X_j. For each t in I, let m_t be the multiplicity of t in the finite multiset lambda. Because I is finite, the multiset lambda is uniquely determined by the tuple (m_t) indexed by t in I. Also,
wt(lambda) = sum_{t in I} t m_t = j - sum_{s in S}(r+s).
Now r >= 0, and every s in I satisfies s >= a+1 >= 1, so each term r+s is nonnegative. Therefore sum_{s in S}(r+s) >= 0, and hence wt(lambda) <= j.

For each t in I we have t >= 1, so
0 <= m_t <= t m_t <= sum_{u in I} u m_u = wt(lambda) <= j.
Thus each m_t is an integer in {0,1,...,j}. Since I has b-a elements, there are at most (j+1)^(b-a) possible tuples (m_t), and therefore at most (j+1)^(b-a) possible multisets lambda for this fixed S. Since there are only finitely many choices of S, we obtain
|X_j| <= 2^(b-a) (j+1)^(b-a) < infinity.
So X_j is finite.

Now define
X_j^even = {(S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even}
and
X_j^odd = {(S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd}.
These two sets are disjoint and their union is X_j. By the definitions of E_j and O_j, we have |X_j^even| = E_j and |X_j^odd| = O_j.

Because X_j is finite, we may split the finite sum over X_j according to this partition:
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|}
= sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^even} (-1)^{|S|} + sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^odd} (-1)^{|S|}.
If (S,lambda) lies in X_j^even, then (-1)^{|S|} = 1. If (S,lambda) lies in X_j^odd, then (-1)^{|S|} = -1. Hence
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|}
= sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^even} 1 + sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^odd} (-1)
= |X_j^even| - |X_j^odd|
= E_j - O_j.
This is exactly the claimed identity.

5. lem_20260329120759_449f1aa9: Let X be a finite set, and let p : X -> {0,1} be a function. Assume that the number of elements x in X with p(x) = 0 is at least the number of elements x in X with p(x) = 1. Then there exists a map iota : X -> X such that iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X, and such that: if iota(x) != x, then p(iota(x)) = 1 - p(x); and if iota(x) = x, then p(x) = 0.
Let
Z := {x in X : p(x) = 0}
and
O := {x in X : p(x) = 1}.
Because p maps X into {0,1}, every element of X lies in exactly one of Z or O. Thus X = Z ∪ O and Z ∩ O = ∅.

Since X is finite, the subsets Z and O are finite. Write
O = {o_1, ..., o_m},
Z = {z_1, ..., z_n},
for some integers m,n >= 0. The hypothesis says that the number of zero-labeled elements is at least the number of one-labeled elements, so n >= m.

Now define a map iota : X -> X as follows:
- for 1 <= i <= m, set iota(o_i) = z_i;
- for 1 <= i <= m, set iota(z_i) = o_i;
- for m < j <= n, set iota(z_j) = z_j.

This is well-defined because O and Z are disjoint, and every element of X is either some o_i or some z_j.

We check that iota is an involution.
- If x = o_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(z_i) = o_i = x.
- If x = z_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(o_i) = z_i = x.
- If x = z_j with m < j <= n, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(z_j) = z_j = x.
Hence iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X.

Next, suppose iota(x) != x. Then x is in one of the first two cases above.
- If x = o_i, then iota(x) = z_i, so
  p(iota(x)) = p(z_i) = 0 = 1 - 1 = 1 - p(o_i) = 1 - p(x).
- If x = z_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(x) = o_i, so
  p(iota(x)) = p(o_i) = 1 = 1 - 0 = 1 - p(z_i) = 1 - p(x).
Thus whenever iota(x) != x, we have p(iota(x)) = 1 - p(x).

Finally, if iota(x) = x, then x cannot be any o_i and cannot be any z_i with 1 <= i <= m; therefore x = z_j for some j with m < j <= n. Hence p(x) = 0.

So iota is an involution on X, every moved point is matched with a point of opposite label, and every fixed point has label 0. This is exactly the required conclusion.

decomposition.strategy_summary: Realize the interval product as the Hilbert series of a graded complete intersection in a weighted polynomial ring. The divisibility-count hypothesis is used only in one bottleneck algebraic realization lemma. Once that realization is available, the coefficient of q^j becomes a graded dimension and is therefore nonnegative. A separate expansion lemma identifies the same coefficient with the signed count of X_j, and a finite-set pairing lemma converts the resulting excess of even-parity elements into the required involution on X_j.

Target: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2). Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|, and assume M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j such that: (1) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then |S'| is congruent to |S| + 1 modulo 2; and (2) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then |S| is even.

Assembly skeleton: Use the divisibility inequalities only once, through the bottleneck realization lemma L1, to build a weighted complete intersection A whose Hilbert series is exactly the interval product in the theorem. By L2, the coefficient of q^j in that product is dim_Q A_j, hence is a nonnegative integer. Independently, L3 expands the same coefficient as the signed sum over X_j with sign (-1)^{|S|}. Lemma L4 rewrites that signed sum as E_j - O_j, where E_j and O_j count elements of X_j with even and odd subset parity respectively; therefore E_j >= O_j. Finally, L5 is a pure finite-set pairing lemma: whenever a finite set has at least as many 0-labeled elements as 1-labeled elements, one can pair every 1-labeled element with a distinct 0-labeled element and leave only 0-labeled fixed points. Applying it to X_j with label p(S,lambda)=|S| mod 2 produces the required involution iota_j. The theorem follows after unpacking the meaning of p.

1. lem_20260329120647_c4ea7dea: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}, and let R := Q[x_s : s in I] be the polynomial ring graded by deg(x_s) = s for each s in I. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. Assume M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Then there exists a family (f_s)_{s in I} of homogeneous polynomials in R such that deg(f_s) = r+s for every s in I, and the ordered list of these polynomials in increasing order of s is a regular sequence in R. If I is empty, this means the empty family.

2. lem_20260329120705_7e7a087b: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}, let R := Q[x_s : s in I] be graded by deg(x_s) = s, and let (f_s)_{s in I} be a family of homogeneous polynomials in R such that deg(f_s) = r+s for every s in I and the ordered list by increasing s is a regular sequence. Put A := R / (f_s : s in I), and let A_n denote the degree-n homogeneous component of A. Then A is a finite-dimensional graded Q-algebra and its Hilbert series is
Hilb_A(q) = sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) q^n = product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)).
In particular, for every integer j >= 0, the coefficient [q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) equals dim_Q A_j and is a nonnegative integer.
Let J_t := (f_s : a+1 <= s <= t) for t = a, a+1, ..., b, with J_a := (0), and let B_t := R/J_t. Then B_a = R and B_b = A. Since every f_s is homogeneous, each J_t is a homogeneous ideal, so each B_t is a graded Q-algebra. Also each degree piece (B_t)_n is finite-dimensional over Q because it is a quotient of R_n.\n\nFirst compute the Hilbert series of R. The monomials product_{s=a+1}^b x_s^{e_s}, with e_s in Z_{>=0}, form a Q-basis of R, and such a monomial has degree sum_{s=a+1}^b s e_s. Hence R_n has basis indexed by tuples (e_s) with sum s e_s = n; there are only finitely many such tuples because all s are positive. Therefore\nHilb_R(q) = sum_{(e_s)} q^(sum s e_s)\n= product_{s=a+1}^b (sum_{m >= 0} q^(m s))\n= product_{s=a+1}^b 1/(1 - q^s).\n\nNow fix t with a+1 <= t <= b, and put d_t := r + t. Since t >= a+1 >= 1 and r >= 0, we have d_t > 0. Because the ordered list (f_{a+1}, f_{a+2}, ..., f_b) is a regular sequence, the class of f_t in B_{t-1} is a non-zero-divisor. Moreover B_t = B_{t-1}/(f_t), where (f_t) now denotes the ideal of B_{t-1} generated by the class of f_t. Since f_t is homogeneous of degree d_t, for each n >= 0 the degree-n part of that ideal is exactly f_t (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t}, with the convention (B_{t-1})_m = 0 for m < 0. Thus for each n >= 0 we have an exact sequence of Q-vector spaces\n0 -> (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t} -- multiplication by f_t -> (B_{t-1})_n -> (B_t)_n -> 0.\nTherefore\ndim_Q (B_t)_n = dim_Q (B_{t-1})_n - dim_Q (B_{t-1})_{n-d_t}.\nSumming over n >= 0 gives\nHilb_{B_t}(q) = (1 - q^(d_t)) Hilb_{B_{t-1}}(q).\n\nIterating this identity from t = a+1 up to t = b, and using the formula for Hilb_R(q), we obtain\nHilb_A(q) = Hilb_{B_b}(q)\n= (product_{s=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+s))) Hilb_R(q)\n= product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)).\n\nBy the definition of Hilbert series, this means that for every j >= 0, the coefficient of q^j in product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)) is exactly dim_Q A_j. In particular, every such coefficient is a nonnegative integer.\n\nIt remains to prove that A is finite-dimensional. For any real u with 0 < u < 1, the series sum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) u^n converges because dim_Q A_n <= dim_Q R_n and\nsum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q R_n) u^n = product_{s=a+1}^b 1/(1 - u^s) < infinity.\nSo we may evaluate the identity above at such a real u:\nsum_{n >= 0} (dim_Q A_n) u^n = product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - u^(r+s))/(1 - u^s)).\n\nFor each fixed s,\n(1 - u^m)/(1 - u) = 1 + u + ... + u^(m-1),\nso\nlim_{u -> 1^-} (1 - u^(r+s))/(1 - u^s) = (r+s)/s.\nHence the right-hand side has a finite limit product_{s=a+1}^b ((r+s)/s) as u -> 1^-; in particular it stays bounded near u = 1.\n\nSuppose, for contradiction, that A_n != 0 for infinitely many n. Then there are infinitely many n with a_n := dim_Q A_n >= 1. Given any positive integer N, choose distinct indices n_1 < ... < n_N with a_{n_i} >= 1. For u sufficiently close to 1, we have u^{n_i} > 1/2 for all i, and then\nsum_{n >= 0} a_n u^n >= sum_{i=1}^N u^{n_i} > N/2.\nSince N is arbitrary, the left-hand side would be unbounded as u -> 1^-, contradicting the boundedness of the right-hand side. Therefore A_n = 0 for all but finitely many n. As each A_n is finite-dimensional, A = direct sum_{n >= 0} A_n is finite-dimensional over Q.\n\nThus A is a finite-dimensional graded Q-algebra, its Hilbert series is exactly product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s))/(1 - q^s)), and the coefficient of q^j in that product is dim_Q A_j and hence a nonnegative integer for every j >= 0.

3. lem_20260329120722_adc74369: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define X_j to be the set of all pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, and wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j, where wt(lambda) denotes the sum of the elements of lambda. Then
[q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|},
where |S| is the cardinality of S.
Let
F(q) := product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = product_{s in I} ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)).
We interpret [q^j] in the formal power series ring Z[[q]]. This is legitimate because every s in I satisfies s >= a+1 >= 1.

For each s in I,
(1 - q^s)^(-1) = sum_{m>=0} q^(ms)
in Z[[q]], since multiplying the right-hand side by 1 - q^s gives 1. Hence
product_{s in I} (1 - q^s)^(-1) = product_{s in I} sum_{m_s>=0} q^(m_s s).
Because I is finite, expanding this finite product gives
product_{s in I} (1 - q^s)^(-1) = sum_{(m_s)_{s in I}} q^(sum_{s in I} m_s s),
where the sum runs over all tuples of nonnegative integers (m_s) indexed by I.

Likewise,
product_{s in I} (1 - q^(r+s))
= sum_{S subseteq I} product_{s in S} (-q^(r+s))
= sum_{S subseteq I} (-1)^{|S|} q^(sum_{s in S} (r+s)).

Multiplying the two expansions, we obtain in Z[[q]]
F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} sum_{(m_s)_{s in I}} (-1)^{|S|} q^( sum_{s in S}(r+s) + sum_{s in I} m_s s ).

Now fix j >= 0. Only finitely many terms on the right can contribute to the coefficient of q^j: the set I is finite, and if sum_{s in I} m_s s <= j then for each s in I we have 0 <= m_s <= j/s. Therefore we may read off the coefficient term-by-term:
[q^j] F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} (-1)^{|S|} * #{ (m_s)_{s in I} : sum_{s in I} m_s s + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }.

For each fixed S, such tuples (m_s) are in bijection with finite multisets lambda of elements of I: m_s is the multiplicity of s in lambda. Under this bijection,
wt(lambda) = sum_{s in I} m_s s.
Therefore
#{ (m_s)_{s in I} : sum_{s in I} m_s s + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }
= #{ lambda : wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j }.
Substituting this into the previous formula gives
[q^j] F(q) = sum_{S subseteq I} sum_{lambda : wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j} (-1)^{|S|}.
But by definition, the pairs (S, lambda) appearing in this double sum are exactly the elements of X_j. Hence
[q^j] product_{s=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+s)) / (1 - q^s)) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|},
as required.

4. lem_20260329120747_f3501562: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define X_j to be the set of all pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, and wt(lambda) + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j, where wt(lambda) is the sum of the elements of lambda. Then X_j is finite. If E_j is the number of elements (S,lambda) in X_j with |S| even and O_j is the number of elements (S,lambda) in X_j with |S| odd, then
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|} = E_j - O_j.
Since 0 <= a <= b, the set I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b} has exactly b-a elements, so I is finite. Hence there are only finitely many subsets S of I, in fact exactly 2^(b-a) of them.

Fix one such subset S. Suppose (S, lambda) is in X_j. For each t in I, let m_t be the multiplicity of t in the finite multiset lambda. Because I is finite, the multiset lambda is uniquely determined by the tuple (m_t) indexed by t in I. Also,
wt(lambda) = sum_{t in I} t m_t = j - sum_{s in S}(r+s).
Now r >= 0, and every s in I satisfies s >= a+1 >= 1, so each term r+s is nonnegative. Therefore sum_{s in S}(r+s) >= 0, and hence wt(lambda) <= j.

For each t in I we have t >= 1, so
0 <= m_t <= t m_t <= sum_{u in I} u m_u = wt(lambda) <= j.
Thus each m_t is an integer in {0,1,...,j}. Since I has b-a elements, there are at most (j+1)^(b-a) possible tuples (m_t), and therefore at most (j+1)^(b-a) possible multisets lambda for this fixed S. Since there are only finitely many choices of S, we obtain
|X_j| <= 2^(b-a) (j+1)^(b-a) < infinity.
So X_j is finite.

Now define
X_j^even = {(S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even}
and
X_j^odd = {(S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd}.
These two sets are disjoint and their union is X_j. By the definitions of E_j and O_j, we have |X_j^even| = E_j and |X_j^odd| = O_j.

Because X_j is finite, we may split the finite sum over X_j according to this partition:
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|}
= sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^even} (-1)^{|S|} + sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^odd} (-1)^{|S|}.
If (S,lambda) lies in X_j^even, then (-1)^{|S|} = 1. If (S,lambda) lies in X_j^odd, then (-1)^{|S|} = -1. Hence
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^{|S|}
= sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^even} 1 + sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j^odd} (-1)
= |X_j^even| - |X_j^odd|
= E_j - O_j.
This is exactly the claimed identity.

5. lem_20260329120759_449f1aa9: Let X be a finite set, and let p : X -> {0,1} be a function. Assume that the number of elements x in X with p(x) = 0 is at least the number of elements x in X with p(x) = 1. Then there exists a map iota : X -> X such that iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X, and such that: if iota(x) != x, then p(iota(x)) = 1 - p(x); and if iota(x) = x, then p(x) = 0.
Let
Z := {x in X : p(x) = 0}
and
O := {x in X : p(x) = 1}.
Because p maps X into {0,1}, every element of X lies in exactly one of Z or O. Thus X = Z ∪ O and Z ∩ O = ∅.

Since X is finite, the subsets Z and O are finite. Write
O = {o_1, ..., o_m},
Z = {z_1, ..., z_n},
for some integers m,n >= 0. The hypothesis says that the number of zero-labeled elements is at least the number of one-labeled elements, so n >= m.

Now define a map iota : X -> X as follows:
- for 1 <= i <= m, set iota(o_i) = z_i;
- for 1 <= i <= m, set iota(z_i) = o_i;
- for m < j <= n, set iota(z_j) = z_j.

This is well-defined because O and Z are disjoint, and every element of X is either some o_i or some z_j.

We check that iota is an involution.
- If x = o_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(z_i) = o_i = x.
- If x = z_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(o_i) = z_i = x.
- If x = z_j with m < j <= n, then iota(iota(x)) = iota(z_j) = z_j = x.
Hence iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X.

Next, suppose iota(x) != x. Then x is in one of the first two cases above.
- If x = o_i, then iota(x) = z_i, so
  p(iota(x)) = p(z_i) = 0 = 1 - 1 = 1 - p(o_i) = 1 - p(x).
- If x = z_i with 1 <= i <= m, then iota(x) = o_i, so
  p(iota(x)) = p(o_i) = 1 = 1 - 0 = 1 - p(z_i) = 1 - p(x).
Thus whenever iota(x) != x, we have p(iota(x)) = 1 - p(x).

Finally, if iota(x) = x, then x cannot be any o_i and cannot be any z_i with 1 <= i <= m; therefore x = z_j for some j with m < j <= n. Hence p(x) = 0.

So iota is an involution on X, every moved point is matched with a point of opposite label, and every fixed point has label 0. This is exactly the required conclusion.
